label: Review of Set Theory
notes: This appendix runs across printed pages 381 to 394 and fixes the working language that every topology chapter reuses. The recurring habit is to translate each claim into a membership test, so that unions, products, quotients, and countability arguments can be checked locally on an arbitrary element.

label: Sets and Membership
notes: A set is determined entirely by which elements belong to it, so equality means matching membership status across the whole ambient universe. Complements only make sense once that universe is declared, which is why specification always carves a new set out of an already available ambient set.

label: Operations and De Morgan
notes: Union, intersection, difference, and complement are Boolean operations on membership predicates, turning distributive and De Morgan laws into row-by-row truth-table identities. Verifying them on a finite universe exposes the same local logic that an infinite proof applies one arbitrary element at a time.

label: Ordered Pairs and Products
notes: An ordered pair remembers a first and second coordinate, unlike an unordered set, and the Cartesian product collects every such pair. Projection maps recover the coordinates, and the product cardinality multiplies, which is exactly why product spaces multiply the choices available later in topology.

label: Relations
notes: A relation on a set is simply a subset of the Cartesian square, broad enough to encode adjacency, containment, or identification. Adjectives like reflexive, symmetric, transitive, and antisymmetric are extra tests on the ordered pairs, and each adjective restricts which structures the relation can describe.

label: Equivalence and Partitions
notes: An equivalence relation is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive, and its classes partition the set into nonempty, pairwise disjoint, covering pieces. In a finite generated model the classes are precisely the connected components, and the quotient set is nothing more mysterious than the collection of those classes.

label: Partial Orders
notes: A partial order is reflexive, transitive, and antisymmetric, with subset inclusion on a power set as the model to remember. The Hasse diagram makes incomparability visible and clarifies the trap that a maximal element, having nothing strictly above it, need not be a maximum above everything.

label: Functions
notes: A function assigns exactly one codomain output to every domain input, and both domain and codomain are part of the data. Injectivity means distinct inputs give distinct outputs, surjectivity means every output is attained, and a bijection, being both, is exactly what an inverse function requires.

label: Images and Preimages
notes: Images push subsets of the domain forward while preimages pull subsets of the codomain back. Preimages commute with union, intersection, and difference because membership reduces to the predicate that the image lies in the target set, whereas images only reliably preserve unions, failing intersections without injectivity.

label: Indexed Families and Disjoint Unions
notes: An indexed family is a function from an index set, and arbitrary unions and intersections quantify membership over that index. Tagging elements with their index builds an abstract disjoint union, keeping equal looking points in separate copies, which is the construction behind later wedge and coproduct spaces.

label: Countability and Cardinality
notes: Two sets share cardinality when a bijection exists, which for infinite sets becomes a constructive listing problem. The diagonal enumeration of the integer lattice and the reduced fraction listing of the rationals show countability, while Cantor diagonalization shows the reals are strictly uncountable.

label: Choice, Zorn, Well-Ordering
notes: The Axiom of Choice supplies a simultaneous selection from arbitrarily many nonempty sets, and it is logically equivalent to Zorn's lemma and to the well-ordering theorem. These tools justify maximal ideals, bases of vector spaces, and the existence proofs that recur throughout the topology chapters.
